key_insight: Medical LLMs stayed highly accurate overall, but became less reliable when physicians framed the request as doubting the correct diagnosis.
clinical_relevance: For second-opinion use in clinical settings, how a doctor asks the question can meaningfully change the model’s answer even when the case facts are unchanged.
method: Preregistered factorial prompting study on 499 MedQA-derived cases.
Three state-of-the-art LLMs were tested across five request styles: neutral, confirmation-seeking, and contradiction-seeking.
Total of 7,485 responses compared accuracy across framing conditions.
evidence_signal: Baseline accuracy was 93.79%, but dropped to 88.51% when physicians expressed doubt about the correct answer (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.43-0.61; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001).
watch_item: Results come from benchmark-style cases, so real-world clinical performance may differ, especially in ambiguous cases and in workflows where model confidence could be over-trusted.
paper_title: Physician epistemic framing alters the accuracy of large language models for medical second opinions
